analytic.title: כתב-יד ירושלמי של התורה מן המאה העשירית שהגיהו מישאל בן עוזיאל (כתב-יד ק 3)

biblStruct.note:
A Tenth-century Pentateuchal MS from Jerusalem (MS C3), Corrected by Mishael ben Uzziel
This study is a detailed analysis of the Biblical MS C3, housed in the Karaite synagogue of Cairo (formerly no. 18 in Gottheil's list, JQR, XVII [1905]), based upon the microfilm that has recently become available for researchers in Jerusalem. 1. (a) C3's owner, Nissi ben Fazlan al-Kharaji, lived in Jerusalem in the second half of the tenth century, during the lifetime of the well-known Karaite author Sahal ben Maẓliaḥ. (b) The (second) corrector, Mishael ben Uzziel ben Yosef ben Hillel, who corrected C3 in Jerusalem, on the property of the Karaites, lived during the lifetime of Maẓliaḥ ben Sahal (and after Sahal had died), i.e., at the end of the tenth century or the beginning of the eleventh. C3's corrector is identical with the well-known Mishael ben Uzziel, who wrote the Book of Ḥillufim (on the variants between Ben Asher and Ben Naphtali). Thus, the author MbU lived in Jerusalem at the end of the tenth century / beginning of the eleventh century. (c) C3 itself was written in the tenth century, apparently in the second half, i.e., during the lifetime of the owner noted at the beginning of the MS. It is certainly no later than that date. 2. A detailed comparison of C3 with A (based upon the new witness of A in the Pentateuch, recently discovered by the author) showed that the first hand (= the scribe) of C3 differs considerably from A. There are 691 variants between C3 (first hand) and A in the Pentateuch! The majority are plene-defective variants: 70.5%. There are, however, several other types of variants. The most striking category, quantitatively, is ± waw at the beginning of a word: 15.8%. The other categories, which occur in much smaller quantities, are: ± letter, ± word, different letter, similar letter (waw-yod), qeriketiv, different word, metathesis. This quantity and quality of variants differ considerably from those found in the well-known 'accurate Tiberian MSS' (e.g., S with about 20 variants, L with 120 variants; with over 99% of these being plene-defective variants). Concentrating, on the other hand, on C3 after it left the hands of the massorete and Mishael ben Uzziel, we find that the massorete had corrected the vast majority of the above textual variants (97%), and later Mishael corrected a few more variants (2%). The massorete based his corrections on an accurate Bible MS (or MSS) accompanied by massorah: 46% of his corrections are accompanied by massoretic notes in the margin of the MS. However, A was not necessarily the MS he used. There are 8 variants between C3 and A that were not corrected by the massorete or Mishael (7 plene defective, one different letter). Thus, from amongst all the known 'accurate Tiberian MSS', C3—second hand (and third hand) is the MS whose text is closest to the Aleppo Codex in the Pentateuch! 3. C3-first hand is similar to a group of MSS from the tenth-eleventh centuries written in the East, like N, L18 (Prophets), whose text differs considerably from the Aleppo Codex, mainly in plene-defective variants. However, C3-first hand is the first example of a Pentateuchal text of this type. The type of MS upon which C3-first hand is based served as one of the sources for the many variants in the later mediaeval Ashkenazi Bible MSS. Thus, the mediaeval MSS (as listed in the apparatus of variants in Kennicott's Bible edition) closest to C3-first hand's 200 variants in Deuteronomy are Ashkenazi MSS, with a large group showing 31%–50% concurrence. 4. MbU, the corrector of C3, wrote 15 marginal notes in C3 concerning vocalization, accentuation, and ga'ayot, all of which deal with the variants between Ben Asher and Ben Naphtali. In these notes, MbU tends to correct the vocalization and accentuation of C3 that agrees with BN to the opinion of BA, and to note the varying opinion. These notes (except 2–3) agree in content with Mishael ben Uzziel's Book of Ḥillufim, and show that C3's corrector is identical with that author. 5. Comparing the material listed by Mishael in his Book of Ḥillufim with C3, we find that: (a) with regard to the typological differences between BA and BN, C3—first hand (= after it left the hand of the vocalizer) agrees in most cases with BN (e.g., the form בן-נון, with dagesh), but not in all (e.g., not with the form בישראל). (b) With regard to the other differences between BA and BN in the Torah (more than 100), C3-first hand agrees with BN in 50% of the cases. (c) With regard to the agreements between BA and BN versus another opinion (more than 100), C3-first hand agrees with the dissenting opinion in 17% of the cases. Thus, C3-first hand contains a considerable undercurrent of BN's opinion, and even contains a small remnant of opinion that differs from both BA and BN. If, however, we look at C3 after it left the hand of MbU, we find that he methodically corrected almost all of the BN variants to agree with BA's opinion (as reflected in the Book of Ḥillufim), and also corrected most of the cases that differed with the agreements between BA and BN. C3-second hand agrees with BA in 93% of the variants in the Torah, and in 96% of the agreements. Thus, from amongst the known 'accurate Tiberian MSS', C3-second hand is the closest to BA in vocalization and accentuation, as reflected in the Book of Ḥillufim. Our study concludes with a discussion of C3's Open and Closed Sections and C3's Songs (Exod. 15; Deut. 32) in comparison with the Aleppo Codex.
